name: Norway
description: Norway offers expats a high quality of life, a robust welfare system, and a strong economy set against stunning natural landscapes. It is renowned for its commitment to equality, safety, and a healthy work-life balance, making it a desirable destination for professionals and families seeking a stable and inclusive environment.
longdescription: Expat life in Norway is characterized by a high standard of living, supported by a comprehensive social welfare system and a robust economy. The country consistently ranks high in global happiness and quality of life indices, thanks to excellent healthcare, education, and public services. While the cost of living, particularly for housing and daily expenses, is notably high, competitive wages and strong social benefits help to offset these costs for those earning locally. Norwegians value punctuality, personal space, and an egalitarian culture, emphasizing humility, respect, and simplicity. English is widely spoken, especially among younger generations, but learning Norwegian is highly recommended for deeper integration into society and to enhance job prospects. The natural beauty, from fjords to the Northern Lights, encourages an active, outdoor lifestyle. However, expats should be prepared for long, dark winters in some regions and a potentially reserved social demeanor initially. The economy is strong, with significant industries in oil and gas, shipping, technology, and renewable energy, as well as demand in healthcare and education. Safety is a paramount feature, with very low crime rates, contributing to a peaceful and secure living environment.

visas.name: Work permit for (Norway)
visas.description: Work permit for skilled workers with a concrete job offer from a Norwegian employer.

visas.name: Norway Student Residence Permit
visas.description: Norway's student residence permit for non-EU/EEA nationals enrolled at a Norwegian university or higher education institution for a full-time programme of study lasting more than 90 days.

visas.name: Norway Family Immigration Permit
visas.description: Norway's family immigration permit allows spouses, cohabiting partners, and minor children of Norwegian residents to join them in Norway, subject to income and integration requirements.

Citizenship by Descent.desc: A child born to a Norwegian mother or father automatically receives Norwegian citizenship at birth, regardless of birthplace, provided the parent was a Norwegian citizen at the time of birth. This applies to children born on or after September 1, 2006. If born before this date, specific rules regarding parental marital status applied. Paternity must be proven if the Norwegian father was not married to the child's mother.

Naturalization.desc: To become a citizen by naturalization, adult foreigners must generally live in Norway for at least 8 years within the last 11 years with valid continuous residence permits of at least one year each. Applicants must be over 12 years old, intend to reside continuously in Norway, achieve a B1 level in spoken Norwegian, pass a social studies/citizenship test, and have no serious criminal record or have completed a waiting period. Exceptions include a reduced residency to 6 years within 10 for those with sufficient income, or 7 years continuous residence for Nordic citizens (via notification).

Birthright.desc: Norway does not have general birthright citizenship (jus soli). Simply being born in Norway does not automatically grant citizenship unless the child would otherwise be stateless (parents have no citizenship or unknown citizenship), or if the child was born in Norway and has lived there until age 18 (facilitated naturalization). The primary path is through a Norwegian parent.

Spouse and Family.desc: Foreign spouses in an official marriage, registered partnership, or cohabitation with Norwegian citizens can obtain citizenship through a '7 years (5+2)' rule: at least 5 years of residence in Norway combined with at least 2 years of marriage to a Norwegian citizen, totaling 7 years in an official relationship. Another rule states a residency of at least 3 years within the past 10 years, provided the marriage has lasted at least 7 years. Applicants must also meet language and citizenship test requirements, have no criminal record, and hold a valid residence permit. Both partners must be at least 24 years old (for family immigration), and intend to live together in Norway.

tax_advice:
*   **Personal Income Tax:** Norway has a progressive income tax system. It consists of a 22% flat rate on ordinary income (wages, dividends, capital gains, pension) and a progressive bracket tax (trinnskatt) ranging from 0.51% to 19.4% on gross income. The effective combined rate for employment income can reach up to 47.4% for high earners.
*   **Wealth Tax (Formuesskatt):** Norway maintains a wealth tax of 1% (municipal) plus 0.3% (national) on net wealth above NOK 1.7 million (approximately $160,000 USD) per person, with the state rate rising to 0.75% on net wealth above NOK 21.5 million.
*   **Employee Social Contributions (Trygdeavgift):** Employees pay 7.9% on wages (reduced by 0.1% in 2026).
*   **Tax Residency:** Tax residency is generally triggered after 183 days in Norway within any 12-month period, or immediately if there's an intent to stay permanently. Once a tax resident, individuals are taxed on their worldwide income and wealth.
*   **PAYE Scheme (Kildeskattordning):** A simplified tax regime for foreign workers on short-term assignments (less than 183 days in any 12-month period) allows for a fixed 25% tax rate on gross Norwegian income, with no deductions and no requirement to file an annual tax return. This scheme applies to non-tax-resident workers earning under NOK 725,050 (2026 threshold).
*   **VAT (Merverdiavgift):** While not explicitly detailed in the provided snippets for a specific percentage for 2026, Norway generally has a high VAT rate, contributing to the high cost of goods and services.
*   **Corporate Tax:** Not explicitly detailed in the provided search results; however, general tax advice often includes corporate tax as a standard policy.
*   **Dual Citizenship and Tax:** Norway allows dual citizenship since 2020. This means individuals applying for Norwegian citizenship are generally no longer required to renounce their existing citizenship.
local_tips:
*   **Cost of Living:** Norway is consistently ranked as one of the world's most expensive countries. Housing, groceries, transportation, and dining out are notably pricey, especially in major cities like Oslo. A single person's estimated monthly costs are around $2,708 USD (approximately 34,097 NOK), excluding rent. A family of four's estimated monthly costs are around $4,853.3 USD (approximately 48,351.3 NOK), excluding rent.
*   **Language:** While many Norwegians speak fluent English, learning Norwegian (aim for B1 level for citizenship) is crucial for deeper social integration and enhancing job opportunities.
*   **Safety:** Norway is a very safe country with low crime rates. Residents enjoy a high level of public safety.
*   **Registration:** Upon moving, expats will need to register with the National Registry to obtain a 'personnummer' (national identification number), which is essential for banking, healthcare, and other public services.
*   **Healthcare:** Norway has a universal healthcare system. Public healthcare is free for those aged 16 and younger, and for pregnant/nursing women. Others pay an annual deductible (approximately 3,278 NOK or $335 USD in 2026), after which they receive an exemption card for free healthcare for the rest of the year.
*   **Work-Life Balance:** Norway is known for its excellent work-life balance, including generous parental leave policies, ample vacation time (five weeks paid vacation annually), and a standard 37.5-hour work week.
*   **Cultural Adaptation:** Norwegians can appear reserved initially, but are generally welcoming and open-minded. Punctuality and personal space are valued. Embracing outdoor activities is a good way to adapt to the climate and local lifestyle.
